Culture.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
Culture.summary: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon.
